'''''Oxalis triangularis''''', commonly called '''false shamrock''', is a species of [[perennial]] [[plant]] in the family [[Oxalidaceae]]. It is native to several countries in southern [[South America]]. This [[woodsorrel]] is typically grown as a [[houseplant]] but can be grown outside in USDA [[Hardiness zone|climate zones]] 8a–11, preferably in light shade.
 
The deep maroon leaves are [[trifoliate]], like species in the clover genus ''[[Trifolium]]'' which are commonly called [[shamrock]], hence the name "false shamrock". The leaves fold down at night, when disturbed, and when in harsh sunlight. The white or pale pink five-petalled flowers also close at night.
 
==Description==
Growing to {{convert|50|cm|in|abbr=on}} tall and broad, the [[subspecies]] ''O. triangularis'' subsp. ''papilionacea'', the purpleleaf false shamrock, is hardy in mild and coastal areas of Britain, down to {{convert| -5|C|F|abbr=on}}, and has won the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/63222/i-Oxalis-triangularis-i-subsp-i-papilionacea-i/Details| title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Oxalis triangularis'' subsp. ''papilionacea'' | access-date = 16 April 2018}}</ref> It is a [[perennial plant]] without aerial stem, formed by leaves borne by a long petiole emerging at the ground level of a tuberous [[rhizome]] (5 cm long, over 10 – 15  mm in diameter, fully covered with scales). The leaf is formed of three [[sessility (botany)|sessile]] leaflets, obtriangular to [[obovate]]-triangular, glabrous, arranged in the same plane perpendicular to the petiole.<ref>Guy L. Nesom: Taxonomic notes on acaculate oxalis (Oxalidaceae) in the United States. In: Phytologia, Volume 91, Issue 3, December 2009.</ref>
 
The five densely haired [[sepal]]s are 5 to 5.5 mm long, narrow and slightly reddish at the top. The five white petals are about 2 inches long and oblong-[[lanceolate]]. The stamens and the [[style (botany)|style]] are densely hairy. The limb of the wild species is green but purple cultivars have been selected for horticulture. The petiole, soft, whitish, is 15 to 25 cm long. Flowering takes place from spring to autumn.
 
===Movement===
[[File:Oxalis Triangularis Photonasty Timelapse.ogv|thumb|A timelapse of the leaves of ''O. triangularis'' closing at night. The recording is at ~750x actual speed and covers a 1.5 hr period of time.]]
The leaves of ''O. triangularis'' move in response to [[light]] levels, opening in high ambient light (in the day) and closing at low light levels (at night). During this movement, the leaflets fold at the level of the central vein. This movement is not due to [[cell growth|growth]] and is instead powered by changes in [[turgor pressure]] in cells at the base of the leaf. It is an example of [[photonasty]].
 
==Range==
The species is distributed in several countries of South America: Brazil, Bolivia, Argentina, and Paraguay. It is a [[neophyte (botany)|neophyte]] in the United States in the states of Florida and Louisiana. It is also widely found in East India, abundantly in states like [[Nagaland]] and Manipur.

==Cultivation and life cycle==
[[File:(MHNT) Oxalis triangularis - Leaves.jpg|thumb|Leaves]]
[[File:Oxalis_triangularis_-_DSCN0066.JPG|thumb|Ornamental shape with red leaves]]
''Oxalis triangularis'' requires bright indirect sunlight supplemented with a cool indoor temperature of {{convert|15|C|F|abbr=on}}. It can tolerate higher indoor temperatures, but will go into dormancy prematurely and/or begin to take on a "tired" appearance if temperatures exceed {{convert|27|C|F|abbr=on}} for prolonged periods of time. It thrives in an average [[potting soil]] with good drainage.
 
Mature plants are cut back to the soil every 3–5 years in early summer or during the dormancy period.  Young plants are cut back to the soil every year in early summer or during the dormancy period, until they reach maturity. To avoid frost, they are usually grown indoors in some regions. They are planted in soil rich in [[humus]] and well-drained. They should be watered only when the topsoil looks dry. In winter, they should not be watered.<ref>Flora of Peru (Volume 2) . In: J. Francis Macbride (ed.): Botanical Series . Volume III, No. 2 . Publication (Field Museum of Natural History), Chicago 1949, pp. 83–84</ref> 

The main difficulty in caring for frost-resistant oxalises is to prevent them from growing uncontrollably.<ref name="StopPoisoning">{{Cite web|title=Five Reasons it's Okay to Love Oxalis – and Stop Poisoning It|url=https://sfforest.org/2015/05/11/five-reasons-its-okay-to-love-oxalis-and-stop-poisoning-it/|accessdate=2022-11-08|work=sfforest.org|date=12 May 2015 }}</ref> The ripe fruit of the plant will crack, throwing out seeds over a considerable distance, so it should not be planted close to vegetable beds.

Oxalis need no fertilizer before flowering. Afterwards it can be supplemented with an appropriate fertilizer. Plants usually only need nitrogen but phosphorus, potassium, and easily absorbed trace elements help them to flower long and beautifully.<ref>{{Cite web|title=How to Grow and Care for Purple Shamrock (False Shamrock)|url=https://www.thespruce.com/purple-shamrock-plants-2132875|accessdate=2022-11-08|work=thespruce.com}}</ref> When growing in a flowerbed,<ref>{{Cite web|title=How to Grow, Repot, and Care For Oxalis Triangularis (False Shamrock)|url=https://www.enterneverland.com/blog/c/indoor/how-to-grow-repot-and-care-for-oxalis-triangularis-false-shamrock|accessdate=2022-11-08|work=enterneverland.com|archive-date=2022-11-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221108105756/https://www.enterneverland.com/blog/c/indoor/how-to-grow-repot-and-care-for-oxalis-triangularis-false-shamrock|url-status=dead}}</ref> it is also worth feeding oxalis during the flowering period with a small dose of a multi-component fertilizer.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Oxalis control|url=https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/oxalis-control/|accessdate=2022-11-08|work=hgic.clemson.edu}}</ref>
 
The [[subspecies]] ''Oxalis triangularis'' subsp. ''papilionacea'' has won the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/63222/Oxalis-triangularis-subsp-papilionacea/Details | title = ''Oxalis triangularis'' subsp. ''papilionacea'' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 18 January 2021}}</ref> 
 
===Usage===

The leaves and flowers are edible but should be used in moderation. Toxicity can occur if large quantities are ingested due to the presence of soluble calcium oxalates. <ref name="Coyne">{{cite web |title=Oxalis triangularis Common Name(s): False Shamrock, Love Plant Purple, Shamrock, Purple Wood Sorrel 
 |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/oxalis-triangularis/#poison |website=North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |access-date=2024-11-27 |date=27 Nov 2024}}</ref>

Thus, the whole plant is potentially toxic to humans and other animals. In horses it can cause colic and possible kidney failure if large amounts are consumed.<ref name="Coyne"/>

==Propagation==
''Oxalis triangularis'' grows from [[corms]] (also called "bulbils"<ref name="StopPoisoning"/>), propagated by division. Like other corms, it goes through regular dormancy periods; at the end of each period, the corms can be unearthed, offsets cut and replanted in appropriate soil, where they will grow into new plants.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.plantoftheweek.org/week021.shtml |title=''Oxalis regnellii atropurpurea'' - Purple Shamrock |publisher=Plant of the week |access-date=2011-06-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110811034840/http://www.plantoftheweek.org/week021.shtml |archive-date=2011-08-11 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
